newsitem.title: CHINA: China says to postpone exchanges with Denmark.
newsitem.headline: China says to postpone exchanges with Denmark.

text.p: China said on Tuesday it was postponing a planned exchange of visits between Chinese and Danish officials in retaliation against Denmark's decision to table a U.N. motion censuring Beijing's human rights record.

"China ... will delay important exchanges of officials that are under discussion and halt exchanges and cooperation with Denmark on human rights," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing.
Shen did not elaborate on the exchanges of visits and the Danish embassy in Beijing declined to comment.

Shen accused Denmark of interfering in China's internal affairs over its decision to table a resolution in the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva to censure Beijing for its human rights record.
"Denmark ... is interfering in China's internal affairs and hurting the feelings of the Chinese people," Shen said.
He warned that bilateral relations would suffer.
"Denmark ... has set up obstacles to the smooth development of relations between the two countries," he said.
"Sino-Danish relations have been damaged. This is something the Chinese side does not wish to see ... The Chinese side cannot not react," Shen added.

China hoped Denmark would have a change of heart, he said. "We sincerely hope ... Denmark will change its confrontational method and return to the road of dialogue and cooperation on an equal footing."
The resolution is due to come up for a vote in Geneva on Tuesday. China was expected to try to prevent debate on its human rights record by seeking approval of a motion of "no action".
The United States reaffirmed on Monday that it would give full backing to the resolution that called on China to observe human rights and protect the cultural identity of Tibetans.

Western groups have for years been critical of Beijing's handling of Tibet, which was seized by Chinese forces in 1950. Large numbers of ethnic Han Chinese have since settled in the Himalayan region amid concern that Chinese culture was swamping the indigenous way of life.

Although U.S. officials privately expressed confidence that they would win good support, diplomats said a Chinese motion for "no action" on the resolution was likely to be passed easily -- as it was last year.
China, mainly with support from Asian and African members of the commission, has fought off European Union and U.S. efforts to have the U.N. body censure Beijing for the past six years in a row.
In Ottawa, the Canadian government decided on Monday not to support the resolution, arguing that engaging China through bilateral committees and visits would be more effective.

Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said a key factor had been the decision by France, followed by several other Western nations, to stop co-sponsoring the resolution, which has been sponsored by Denmark, the United States and 13 other countries.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has telephoned the German, Spanish and Australian foreign ministers in an effort to prevent China from blocking debate on the resolution, the State Department said on Monday.
Germany, Spain, Italy and Greece have said they could not support the resolution.
